claims.text: The initial alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with minimal pre-existing intermetallic phases.
Isothermal aging at service-relevant temperatures induces diffusion-controlled Mg segregation.
Mg segregation produces Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates nucleate and grow both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
An initially fine and uniform distribution of Mg-rich precipitates promotes formation of a stable protective surface film under oxidizing conditions.
The protective film formed during early aging is enriched in Ti and/or Zn oxides.
Early-stage protective-film formation maintains high oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Continued aging beyond a critical incubation period causes intermetallic precipitate coarsening.
Coarsening of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates disrupts the continuity and integrity of the protective surface film.
Loss of protective-film integrity reduces corrosion resistance.
Loss of protective-film integrity reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Intermetallic evolution is slower or more delayed during aging in argon than during aging in air.
The proposed mechanism operates between 500 °C and 700 °C for aging durations up to 50 hours.
Samples will be compared after aging at 500 °C and 700 °C for 1–50 hours in air versus argon.
In situ high-temperature XRD or real-time microscopy can be used to track intermetallic nucleation and growth kinetics.
Absence of a significant air-versus-argon difference in intermetallic evolution kinetics would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of a correlation between intermetallic coarsening and deterioration of surface-film properties and performance would falsify the hypothesis.
